drills.q: A memory is built from which three parts you already had?
options: A decoder, a row of registers, and a multiplexer
A counter, an adder, and a register
A latch array and an address comparator
A decoder and a set of tri-state buffers only
drills.why: Plus one AND per row to gate the write. There is no fourth idea in this unit.

drills.q: In a memory, the write signal reaches a register:
options: ANDed with that register's own line from the decoder
Directly, with the decoder selecting the output only
Through a comparator against the address
Only when the address changes
drills.why: Exactly one decoder line is high, so exactly one register loads and the rest hold. Leaving the write ungated writes to every register at once.

options: Nowhere. It is wires into a decoder and into a multiplexer
In a tag field alongside each location
In a lookup table in the memory controller
In the first word of each block
drills.why: No register knows its own number. The number identifies a location only in the sense that it is the number that lights that location's line.

drills.q: Reading location 0 compared to location 1000, in this unit's memory:
options: Costs exactly the same
Is faster, because the address is smaller
Is slower, because the decoder starts at zero
Depends on what was read last
drills.why: The same wires carry a different pattern into the same gates. That stops being true the moment there is a cache, and Part V is largely about it stopping.

drills.q: Why are real memories built as trees rather than one flat decode?
options: A wide flat decoder is an impossible fan-in and a wide flat multiplexer
Trees use less power
Flat decoding cannot address more than 256 locations
Trees allow several accesses at once
drills.why: Split the address: high bits choose a block, low bits choose within it. Depth then grows with the logarithm of the size rather than the size.

drills.q: What turns a counter into a program counter?
options: A second input path, so it can be loaded from outside instead of
A wider register
A connection to the instruction decoder
A reset input
drills.why: The increment path means "carry on" and the load path means "go somewhere else". A jump is not a mechanism, it is that load input.

drills.q: Why does a jump cost the same as not jumping in a simple machine?
options: Both are one edge into the same register, with a multiplexer choosing the
Because jumps are predicted
Because the pipeline is flushed either way
It does not; jumps are always slower
drills.why: That stops being true once there is a pipeline, which is Part V, and the reason it stops is worth knowing precisely because it is free here.

options: The same load, with its enable ANDed with a flag
Dedicated branch hardware
A comparison unit
A second program counter
drills.why: Two more wires. The flags they read are the leftovers of an arithmetic operation that already happened.

drills.q: If a location is read and written in the same cycle, the read returns:
options: The old value, because every register shows what it held coming into the
The new value
Whichever happened first
An undefined value
drills.why: That is not a quirk to work around. It is what lets a value be read, passed through an adder and written back to the same place in one cycle.

drills.q: What does static memory store a bit in?
options: A feedback loop of transistors, which holds while the power is on
A capacitor
A magnetic domain
A floating gate
drills.why: Several transistors per bit, which is why a processor has kilobytes of it rather than gigabytes.

drills.q: Why must dynamic memory be refreshed?
options: Its bit is a charge on a capacitor, and a capacitor leaks
The clock drifts
Reading it is destructive and must be undone
The addresses need periodic remapping
drills.why: Leakage is the same phenomenon from unit 001 arriving somewhere else. The memory reads and writes back its own contents continuously, forever, just to keep saying the same thing.

drills.q: One bit of dynamic memory costs roughly:
options: One transistor and one capacitor
Two transistors
Six transistors
One transistor and one resistor
drills.why: Which is why you can have gigabytes of it. Static memory is a dozen transistors a bit and correspondingly faster and more expensive.

options: A memory and a register holding a number, plus an agreement about what
A dedicated last-in-first-out structure
A special addressing mode
A region the processor protects
drills.why: Nothing enforces what the number points to, which is where a whole category of security problem later comes from.

drills.q: What does a linked list look like to the hardware?
options: Some bits in some locations, with an agreement about what they mean
A structure the memory controller follows
A sequence of addresses in a special format
Nothing; lists are a language feature
drills.why: Nothing in memory knows about lists, and nothing in memory knows about anything. That is the same answer as every other "how does it know" in this part.

drills.q: Popping from an empty stack, in this unit's stack pointer:
options: Wraps around, because nothing is checking the range
Raises an error
Holds at zero
Is prevented by the hardware
drills.why: Going down from 0 wraps to the top the same way going up from the top wraps to 0. Every check that a real machine has is something added on top, and each one had to be paid for.
